description: Calculate gas volumes at RTP, atom economy, and percentage yield for chemical reactions.
content_html:
Gas Volumes at Room Temperature and Pressure

At room temperature and pressure (RTP, defined as 25°C and 1 atmosphere), one mole of any gas occupies a volume of 24 dm³. This is called the molar gas volume at RTP. It applies to all gases regardless of their identity — a mole of oxygen takes up the same volume as a mole of carbon dioxide or hydrogen at RTP.

This gives a simple pair of equations:

$$\text{volume (dm}^3\text{)} = n \times 24$$ $$n = \frac{\text{volume (dm}^3\text{)}}{24}$$

If you know the volume in cm³, divide by 24,000 to find moles, or multiply moles by 24,000 to find volume in cm³. Alternatively, divide the cm³ value by 1000 first to convert to dm³, then use the 24 dm³ rule. Keep track of your units — mixing cm³ and dm³ is a common exam error.

Key Fact

Molar gas volume at RTP = 24 dm³/mol. Volume (dm³) = moles × 24. Moles = volume (dm³) ÷ 24. Always check whether your volume is in cm³ (divide by 1000) or dm³ before using this equation.

Excess zinc is added to 5.0 g of sulfuric acid (H&sub2;SO&sub4;). Calculate the volume of hydrogen gas produced at RTP.

The reaction is: \(\text{Zn} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4 + \text{H}_2\)

Step 1: Mr of H&sub2;SO&sub4; = (2 × 1) + 32 + (4 × 16) = 98 g/mol.

Step 2: Moles of H&sub2;SO&sub4; = \(\frac{5.0}{98} = 0.0510\) mol (3 s.f.).

Step 3: Mole ratio. The equation shows 1 mol H&sub2;SO&sub4; produces 1 mol H&sub2;, so moles of H&sub2; = 0.0510 mol.

Step 4: Volume = 0.0510 × 24 = 1.22 dm³ (or 1220 cm³).

Percentage Yield

In practice, chemical reactions rarely produce as much product as the theoretical calculation predicts. This is because the reaction may not go to completion, some product may be lost during purification, or there may be competing side reactions. The ratio of actual yield to theoretical yield is the percentage yield:

$$\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield (g)}}{\text{theoretical yield (g)}} \times 100$$

Percentage yield is always between 0% and 100%. A 100% yield is essentially impossible in practice. High yields are desirable in industrial chemistry because they reduce waste and improve profitability. Factors that reduce yield include: reversible reactions reaching equilibrium before completion, loss of product during filtration or evaporation, and formation of by-products.

12.0 g of magnesium is burned in excess oxygen. The theoretical yield of magnesium oxide (MgO) is 20.0 g. The student collects 16.8 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

Step 1: Identify actual yield = 16.8 g, theoretical yield = 20.0 g.

Step 2: \(\text{percentage yield} = \frac{16.8}{20.0} \times 100 = 84\%\)

The yield is 84% — this could be because some MgO was lost when collected, or some Mg did not react fully.

Atom Economy

Atom economy measures how efficiently a reaction uses its reactant atoms. It does not depend on the actual amounts used — it is a property of the reaction equation itself. The equation is:

$$\text{atom economy (\%)} = \frac{M_r \text{ of desired product}}{\text{sum of } M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100$$

A reaction with 100% atom economy produces only the desired product and no by-products. Addition reactions (where two molecules join to form one product) have 100% atom economy. Substitution or decomposition reactions have lower atom economy because some atoms end up in by-products that may be wasted.

Key Fact

Atom economy depends on the balanced equation (which atoms go to desired product vs by-products). Percentage yield depends on the actual experiment (how much product you collected compared with the maximum possible). Both are expressed as percentages.

Calcium carbonate is heated to produce calcium oxide and carbon dioxide: \(\text{CaCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2\). Calculate the atom economy for calcium oxide (the desired product). [Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16]

Step 1: Mr of CaO = 40 + 16 = 56 g/mol.

Step 2: Sum of Mr of all products = Mr(CaO) + Mr(CO&sub2;) = 56 + (12 + 32) = 56 + 44 = 100.

Step 3: Atom economy = \(\frac{56}{100} \times 100 = 56\%\). The other 44% of atoms end up in CO&sub2;.
exam_tip_html: The most common errors on gas volume questions are forgetting to use 24 dm³/mol (rather than 22.4 dm³/mol, which is the molar volume at 0°C) and not converting cm³ to dm³. For atom economy, use the Mr values from the balanced equation — always divide the Mr of the desired product by the total Mr of all products, not by the reactants. For percentage yield, check you have the fraction the right way round: actual ÷ theoretical (not the other way round). Neither atom economy nor percentage yield has units.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Molar gas volume at RTP = 24 dm³/mol. Volume (dm³) = moles × 24; moles = volume (dm³) ÷ 24. Convert cm³ to dm³ (divide by 1000) before using these equations.
  • Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100. It is always ≤100% because product is always lost in a real experiment.
  • Atom economy = (Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all products) × 100. It is a property of the balanced equation, not the experiment. Addition reactions have 100% atom economy.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the volume of gas produced, at RTP, when 0.25 mol of a gas is released in a reaction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States molar gas volume at RTP = 24 dm³/mol; volume = 0.25 × 24 = 6.0 dm³; units stated.
Secure: Correct calculation; minor unit error.
Developing: Uses 24 but does not state the principle; answer has no units.
Emerging: Recalls 24 but cannot set up the calculation.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the number of moles in 1200 cm³ of carbon dioxide gas at RTP.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Converts 1200 cm³ to 1.200 dm³; n = 1.200 ÷ 24 = 0.0500 mol; units correct.
Secure: Correct method; forgot to convert cm³ to dm³ (n = 1200 ÷ 24 = 50 mol — common error, penalise once).
Developing: Divides by 24 but does not convert volume.
Emerging: Attempts division but incorrect formula.

practice_questions.text: A reaction produces 4.20 g of a product. The maximum theoretical yield was 6.00 g. Calculate the percentage yield.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: percentage yield = (4.20 ÷ 6.00) × 100 = 70.0%; equation stated; values substituted correctly; answer expressed as percentage.
Secure: Correct answer with minor arithmetic error or percentage symbol missing.
Developing: Values correct but inverted (6.00 ÷ 4.20 × 100).
Emerging: Recalls the concept of yield but cannot apply equation.

practice_questions.text: The reaction for the production of ammonia is: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Explain why atom economy for this reaction is 100%.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that atom economy = Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all products × 100; notes there is only one product (NH₃) so all atoms from the reactants end up in the desired product; therefore atom economy = 100%.
Secure: Identifies single product and links to all atoms being in the desired product.
Developing: States atom economy is 100% because no by-products, without explaining what atom economy measures.
Emerging: States the reaction is efficient with no scientific explanation.

practice_questions.text: Iron(III) oxide is reduced with carbon: 2Fe₂O₃ + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for iron. [Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16, C = 12]
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mr of 4Fe = 4 × 56 = 224; Mr of 3CO₂ = 3 × (12 + 32) = 3 × 44 = 132; sum of all products = 224 + 132 = 356; atom economy = (224 ÷ 356) × 100 = 62.9% (3 s.f.); units (%) stated.
Secure: Correct method with one arithmetic error in Mr calculation.
Developing: Divides Mr(Fe) by Mr of reactants rather than all products.
Emerging: Mr of Fe calculated correctly but equation not applied.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a high atom economy is desirable in industrial chemistry, and why 100% percentage yield is not achievable in practice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: High atom economy: reduces waste (fewer by-products to dispose of), more efficient use of raw materials, lower environmental impact, more cost-effective. 100% yield impossible: reactions may be reversible and not go to completion; product is lost during purification/filtration/evaporation; side reactions may consume some reactant; product may remain in solution. Clear distinction between the two concepts maintained.
Secure: Both ideas addressed with at least two valid points each; clear scientific reasoning.
Developing: Atom economy or percentage yield addressed well; the other addressed briefly.
Emerging: One concept partially explained with limited detail.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the molar gas volume at room temperature and pressure (RTP)?
A reaction produces 3.6 g of product. The theoretical yield is 6.0 g. What is the percentage yield?
Atom economy = (Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all _____) × 100.
To find the volume of a gas at RTP in dm³, multiply the number of moles by _____.
Match each term to what it measures:
right: How much product was collected vs the theoretical maximum
Proportion of reactant atoms ending up in the desired product
Volume occupied by one mole of gas at RTP (24 dm³)

flashcard_questions.q: What is the molar gas volume at RTP?
How do you find volume in dm³ from moles using molar gas volume?
How many moles are in 48 dm³ of gas at RTP?
What is the equation for percentage yield?

flashcard_questions.a: No — you cannot collect more product than the theoretical maximum.
The proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product, as a percentage.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of reaction always has 100% atom economy?
flashcard_questions.a: Addition reactions — only one product is formed.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one reason why percentage yield is less than 100% in a real experiment.
flashcard_questions.a: Any one of: reaction doesn't go to completion / product lost during purification / side reactions.

flashcard_questions.q: The atom economy for reaction X is 45%. What does this mean?
flashcard_questions.a: Only 45% of reactant atoms end up in the desired product; 55% become by-products.

flashcard_questions.q: How do you convert a gas volume from cm³ to dm³?

glossary_terms.definition: The volume occupied by one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (RTP). The value is 24 dm³/mol.
The percentage of the theoretical (calculated) maximum amount of product that is actually obtained from a chemical reaction.
A measure of the proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product, calculated as (relative formula mass of desired product ÷ sum of relative formula masses of all products) × 100.
The maximum mass of product that could be obtained from a reaction, calculated from the molar ratios in the balanced equation.
The mass of product that is actually collected at the end of a chemical reaction in a real experiment.
A substance produced alongside the desired product in a chemical reaction, reducing the atom economy of the process.
